case_study_insert.main_stem: Lakestone Fresh Foods (LFF) is a private limited company in the food processing sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2009 by Mara Lakestone, the business supplies chilled ready meals to national supermarket chains and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. LFF plans to invest $850,000 in a new automated ready-meal production line with sustainable eco-packaging, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $255,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.40 a unit and a selling price of $11.50, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. LFF faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 9% and labour turnover is rising, and its warehouse has reported rising food-waste levels.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The ready-meal line packed 22,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 1.8%, down from 3.1% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 38 to 21 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 3.2 days. Market research of 600 supermarket shoppers found that 64% would pay up to $0.40 more for eco-packaged meals, and 52% check packaging sustainability before buying. A training needs analysis shows 20 of 45 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sealing machines; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $900 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Lakestone Fresh Foods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, the fourth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $12.40 to $13.23 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Wholesale dairy and wheat input costs have risen 12.4% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is running at 8.1%, while consumer spending on own-label chilled meals grew 3.5% in the same period.

questions.question_text: LFF plans to finance part of its ready-meal expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for LFF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs LFF nothing in repayments or interest charges, which protects the company's cash flow and profit margin at a time when it already faces fixed costs of $255,000 a year and a $500,000 bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can be used to absorb the 12.4% rise in dairy and wheat input costs, helping LFF stay competitive in supermarket supply without raising prices above the $11.50 selling price.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $350,000 is available without putting LFF's new $850,000 production line at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Mara Lakestone's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how the automated ready-meal line is operated or expanded next.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Lakestone Fresh Foods and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: LFF is launching its new chilled ready-meal range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should LFF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would reach millions of potential buyers very quickly and build strong brand awareness for the new ready-meal range across all supermarkets stocking LFF. However, production and airtime costs are extremely high, and much of the audience would be outside LFF's distribution area or not buy chilled meals, so wastage of spend would be large for a 45-employee business funding an $850,000 expansion.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper than television, reaches LFF's core regional supermarket catchment, and suits time-sensitive messages such as new product launches. Its limitation is narrow reach; the range is supplied to national supermarket chains across the country, so local listeners alone cannot generate the volume needed to justify the 90,000-unit output target.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with food and family lifestyle influencers targets exactly the 64% of 600 surveyed shoppers willing to pay $0.40 more for eco-packaged meals, with measurable engagement and strong appeal to younger supermarket buyers. Results are slower to compound than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but cost per reached shopper is low and the 52% of shoppers who check packaging sustainability can be shown the eco-packaging story directly.

Recommendation: LFF should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment already identified in its research, costs far less than television, scales nationally like radio cannot, and reinforces the eco-packaging positioning. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 45-person manufacturer funding a bank-loan-financed expansion; radio is rejected as too narrow for national supermarket distribution; influencers alone also lack the mass reach of TV, so LFF should layer modest in-store supermarket promotions on top.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of LFF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of LFF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: LFF's absenteeism has reached 9% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for LFF of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 45 employees a genuine voice in how the new ready-meal production line is organised, which satisfies their social and esteem needs (Maslow) and increases job satisfaction. Workers who help set sealing-machine routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking LFF's 9% absenteeism rate and reducing the pressure on its flat structure.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions generates practical suggestions from the people who handle sealed meals daily, improving quality and reducing the 1.8% defect rate further. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving the $900 per employee retraining cost at the local college and protecting output of 90,000 units while the $850,000 automated line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LFF's absenteeism, quality and output.

questions.question_text: LFF must upskill 20 production staff to operate the new sealing machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should LFF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the production line is directly relevant to LFF's own sealing machines and quality standards, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 20 staff productive while they learn, which protects the Q3 output of 22,500 units and the effort behind the falling 1.8% defect rate. Drawbacks are that trainers are production staff whose own work suffers, bad habits can be passed on, and official certification is limited, which may matter if supermarket auditors demand formal records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $900 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 20 staff, costing $18,000 in total — affordable against an $850,000 investment. It removes staff from the line, however, reducing short-term capacity, and the generic content may not match LFF's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be needed.

Decision: LFF should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, supported by short college sessions for the most senior operators. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while absenteeism is already 9%; full off-the-job training is rejected because withholding $18,000 and losing 20 staff from the line would hurt the supermarket delivery schedule, and LFF can add college visits later once the line stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to LFF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of LFF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of LFF with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how LFF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $255,000 ÷ ($11.50 − $6.40) = $255,000 ÷ $5.10 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $11.50 − $6.40 = $5.10. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.10.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways LFF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. LFF's managers can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units to confirm the ready-meal line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 40,000 units, informing whether to ramp up to the new automated capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.10 lets LFF model the effect of a discount negotiated with supermarket chains, for example a 5% price cut to $10.93 would drop contribution to $4.53, letting managers judge whether extra volume would still cover the $255,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $255,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume targets used to justify the $500,000 bank loan repayments and to check the new line can service them before committing further capital.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($255,000 ÷ 90,000 units + $6.40 = $9.23 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, identify waste driving the warehouse food-waste problem, and decide whether to renegotiate the $6.40 variable cost with suppliers amid the 12.4% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.10 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 90,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling vs $255,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $850,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $9.23 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LFF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LFF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.44 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.64 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.20 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $120,000 inventories + $180,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $345,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $205,000 + $60,000 = $360,000. Current ratio 2024 = $345,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.44; 2025 = $360,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.64. Acid test 2024 = ($345,000 − $120,000) ÷ $240,000 = $225,000 ÷ $240,000 = 0.94; 2025 = ($360,000 − $95,000) ÷ $220,000 = $265,000 ÷ $220,000 = 1.20.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. The current ratio improved from 1.44 to 1.64, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $240,000 to $220,000 while assets rose. The acid test, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.94 to 1.20, so LFF no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term debts — critical while it services a $500,000 bank loan and funds an $850,000 expansion. However, trade receivables rose from $180,000 to $205,000, tying up cash; if supermarket customers pay late, the stronger ratios could deteriorate quickly, and inventories fell to $95,000, so stock availability for peak supermarket demand should be monitored.

Conclusion: LFF's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.44 to 1.64) and the acid test ratio (0.94 to 1.20) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so LFF should tighten credit control while proceeding with the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether LFF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LFF of introducing sustainable eco-packaging for its chilled ready-meal range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-packaging matches the preferences of the 64% of shoppers in LFF's market research who would pay up to $0.40 more for such meals, allowing LFF to charge a premium that protects its $5.10 contribution per unit even as input costs rise 12.4%. It also strengthens LFF's brand image with the 52% of shoppers who check packaging sustainability, helping win or retain national supermarket listings for the $850,000 line.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials typically cost more than conventional plastic, which would increase the $6.40 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the $0.40 premium is accepted across the whole range. Any failure in eco-materials (for example, higher breakage or shorter shelf life for chilled meals) would also raise the current 1.8% defect rate and increase food-waste costs before the new production line stabilises.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LFF's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.7% minimum wage increase and the 12.4% rise in input costs will affect LFF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If LFF's $500,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small next to LFF's $255,000 fixed costs, and if the loan was fixed-rate it is zero. Higher base rates may also make consumers more cautious about premium own-label meals and could raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $850,000 expansion. LFF can largely fix this risk now by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.23 per hour): LFF has a workforce of 45 in which most production and packing roles are hourly-paid, so this rise feeds directly into its wage bill and is not optional. The insert does not state hours worked or each worker's pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the correct way to judge it is against LFF's given productivity data: 90,000 units ÷ 45 staff = 2,000 units per worker, so a wage rise is affordable only if productivity holds at that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $5.10 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (12.4% dairy and wheat): LFF's variable cost of $6.40 per unit is dominated by ingredients, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound can be computed honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 12.4% it would add 12.4% × $6.40 = $0.79 per unit; at 90,000 units a year that is roughly $71,000 a year (90,000 × $0.79). Even if only an illustrative $0.50 per unit were added, that is $45,000 a year — cutting contribution per unit from $5.10 toward about $4.30–$4.60. LFF can recover part of it through the $0.40 eco-packaging premium and supermarket price negotiations, both given in its research.

Conclusion: The 12.4% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact: it compounds on every one of the 90,000 units LFF sells, directly eroding the $5.10 contribution that justifies the $850,000 expansion, and it cannot be fixed by doing anything other than negotiating input prices or raising the selling price. The wage rise is the second most serious risk because it is non-negotiable but manageable through productivity of 2,000 units per worker; the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms ($3,750 a year on a variable-rate loan) and can be fixed directly by LFF.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to LFF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LFF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of LFF with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
